teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the energy levels, numbered one, two, three and four, going up in energy. Each level is split into subshells. A subshell is a group of orbitals of the same type and energy. Level one has just an s subshell. Level two has s and p. Level three has s, p and d. And level four has all four types, s, p, d and f. So the level number tells you how many subshell types it has. Each subshell is made of orbitals, the regions where an electron is likely to be found. An s subshell has one orbital, a p subshell has three, a d has five, and an f has seven. Here's the key rule. Each orbital holds at most two electrons, and those two must spin in opposite directions. We draw each orbital as a box, and its electrons as an up arrow and a down arrow. So an s subshell holds two electrons, p holds six, d holds ten, and f holds fourteen. Now the notation itself. Take three p five. The three is the energy level. The p is the type of subshell. And the small raised five is the number of electrons in it. So it's an address. Level three, the p subshell, five electrons live there. A full configuration lists every occupied subshell like this, and the raised numbers always add up to the number of electrons in the atom.

Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
> Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

1. Energy levels (n = 1, 2, 3, 4) split into subshells: level 1: s; level 2: s, p; level 3: s, p, d; level 4: s, p, d, f.
2. Orbitals per subshell: s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins. Capacities: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
3. Notation: 3p⁵ = level 3, p subshell, 5 electrons. Superscripts add up to the number of electrons.

5. Equal-energy orbitals fill one per box before pairing. P: 3 unpaired; Cl: 1 unpaired; Fe: 4 unpaired.

Memory aid (large, on the notes screen): *Lowest first, one per box, then pair, and check the total.*
